title: Necrotising Fasciitis
subject: Surgery
summary: A rapidly progressive, life‑threatening infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and skin changes guide urgent surgical debridement. Early recognition saves lives.

sections.p: Necrotising fasciitis (NF) is a fulminant bacterial infection that destroys fascia and surrounding tissues. It is a surgical emergency; diagnosis is clinical, supported by laboratory and imaging when available.
b: Pain out of proportion to exam

t.b: Leukocytosis indicates systemic response; >25×10^9/L raises concern.
Hyponatraemia (<135 mmol/L) is common in severe NF.
Shows fascial thickening, gas; used if patient stable and resources allow.

sections.p: The Fournier’s classification (I–IV) and the LRINEC score help gauge urgency and guide management. In low‑resource settings, clinical judgment overrides scores.

t.b: Score ≥8 indicates high risk; >6 still warrants high suspicion.

sections.p: Polymicrobial in tropical climates; common organisms include Group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes, and gram‑negative rods. Local factors such as trauma, ulcers, and HIV increase risk.

t.b: Rapid bedside test; gram‑positive cocci suggest GAS; gram‑negative rods suggest polymicrobial.

sections.p: Early signs mimic cellulitis but progress rapidly. Key features: disproportionate pain, swelling, erythema, bullae, skin discoloration, crepitus, and systemic signs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain out of proportion to exam

faq.q: What is the most common organism in NF?
faq.a: Group A Streptococcus, often with anaerobes and gram‑negative rods.

faq.q: Can I wait for imaging before surgery?
faq.a: No; delay increases mortality. Operate on clinical suspicion.
It blocks toxin production and improves outcomes in GAS infections.
